arguments.name: Volume 4 is not an abandonment of resurrection apologetics
arguments.conclusion: Volume 4's focus on theological and practical implications does not mean Habermas has given up on evidential resurrection apologetics.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1 The book has two halves: the first half treats God, miracles, and worldview, and the second half is almost no apologetics by his definition.
P2 Resurrection apologetics still appears here and there, but it is not the concentration of the volume.
P3 The series is built on the evidential case of volume 1 and the reputational/historical case of volume 2, without which volume 4 could not be done at a scholarly level.
P4 Habermas has always been a strict evidentialist and would not do subjective or presuppositionalist apologetics even if paid.

st1.quote: So if the critique is see he's gone over the blank um they don't know they don't know me they don't know where 52 years of teaching

st2.quote: There's there's not a lot of overlap between the 30-ish books all the way from my doctoral dissertation, which has been published um all the way through to these four volumes.

st3.quote: The resurrection argument stands on a evidences volume one, b reputations volume two.

st4.quote: The second half of the book is almost no apologetics by my uh definition.

st5.quote: You may not like my reasons, but don't say I'm not giving reasons.

st6.quote: The first half of the book does talk about God, the miracles question.

st8.quote: The resurrection argument stands on a evidences volume one, b reputations volume two.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Historical Jesus (doctoral work) and volume 1-2 of the resurrection series

or1.quote: The resurrection argument stands on a evidences volume one, b reputations volume two.
or1.why: Restates Habermas's own prior volumes rather than offering a new argument.

arguments.weakest_link: P3 assumes the prior volumes stand, which is exactly what the objection denies.
arguments.develop_next: Give a concrete page/chapter count of resurrection-specific material inside volume 4.

arguments.name: Skeptical objections are unfalsifiable and silly
arguments.conclusion: The objection that volume 4 abandons evidence is not worth answering because radical skeptics will never be satisfied.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1 If skeptics are really skeptical, no answer will make a difference; they will move to another objection or invent a new story.
P2 The objection itself is absurd because Habermas continues to give reasons and evidence.
P3 The critics ignore volumes 1 and 2, which still stand as the evidential foundation.

st1.quote: But I'm just saying those objections are absolutely silly.

st2.quote: If they're really skeptical, no matter what I say will make no difference.

st3.quote: You may not like my reasons, but don't say I'm not giving reasons.

st7.quote: They will either go to something else just as easily or they will make a new story up and act like it was their story all along anyway.

st8.quote: I've known Gary for what 16 years now, 16 years plus, and he he's always been hardcore strict evidentialism

or1.quote: You can't really answer these guys because here's the key.
or1.why: A distinct ad hominem-style dismissal rather than a substantive reply.

arguments.weakest_link: P1 is a psychological generalization about skeptics, not a premise about the objection's truth.
arguments.develop_next: Distinguish the objection's content from the critic's motives and answer the content.

arguments.name: Theism and afterlife are linked
arguments.conclusion: An evidential afterlife case is a strong argument for God because an afterlife cannot be explained by naturalism.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1 Russell's Why I Am Not a Christian treats God and the afterlife as the two things needed for theism.
P2 If there is an afterlife, one must ask why; it does not follow from any naturalism Habermas knows.
P3 An afterlife cannot come from time plus chance plus the natural world.
P4 Therefore an afterlife points to a God who is needed for it.

st1.quote: if you have an afterlife, I think you're gonna I I think you're going to have a problem if you don't see an afterlife is something that a god is needed for.

st2.quote: I don't think an afterlife comes from God plus chance [snorts] plus the supernatural just just to I mean, sorry, time plus chance plus the the natural world.

st3.quote: in that short pretty short book, uh we learn that what you need for theism is God in the afterlife.

st4.quote: I don't think that follows from any naturalism I know.

st5.quote: I think it's probably not a not as strong for God.

st6.quote: I think it's a strong argument, but I think it's once you have an afterlife, you've got to ask why.

st8.quote: It's like the ethical argument, you know, why why do why do objective ethics u come in a chance big bang?

arguments.prior_art: Bertrand Russell, Why I Am Not a Christian, 1927

or1.quote: I appreciated him doing that little bit at the beginning. God and an afterlife.
or1.why: A variant of the standard theistic-argument-from-afterlife, framed via Russell.

or3.quote: It's like the ethical argument, you know, why why do why do objective ethics u come in a chance big bang?
or3.why: Connects afterlife to the moral argument's structure.

arguments.weakest_link: P3 asserts without argument that naturalism cannot produce an afterlife.
arguments.develop_next: Specify what feature of an afterlife (e.g. continued consciousness) naturalism cannot supply.

arguments.name: Resurrection entails God and the deity of Christ
arguments.conclusion: If the resurrection occurred, it entails a God who raised Jesus and links to Jesus' unique claims, including his deity.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1 If there is a resurrection, there must be a God who did it.
P2 No founder of the major world religions was reportedly raised from the dead, nor were Old Testament figures such as Moses, Daniel, or David.
P3 Jesus' leading teaching was the kingdom of God and how to enter it, and he claimed to hold the keys to it.
P4 God would not raise a false teacher from the dead, so Jesus' major teaching must be true.
P5 Jesus' ethical life and claims further support the link to his deity.

st1.quote: If there's a resurrection, I think there's a God.

st2.quote: Moses didn't rise from the dead. Daniel didn't rise from the dead. David didn't rise from the dead.

st3.quote: Even critical scholars, Dale Allison, I mean others, uh, they think it's likely that Jesus foretold his death and resurrection ahead of time.

st4.quote: God doesn't wouldn't raise a heretic from the dead.

st5.quote: some people say, just give you one example, that Buddha, our sources for Buddha are so late as to even say he said anything.

st6.quote: If pre if he preached good e ethics and yet his major teaching the kingdom of God how to get there was false. seems to me that the major the falseness of the major rules out the truth the truth of the minor.

st8.quote: Probably I think the best text for Jesus claiming to be deity is Mark 14:61-64.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Risen Jesus and Future Hope, 2003

or1.quote: If there's a resurrection, somebody had to do it. the somebody had to be linked with Jesus's claims in my view because nobody else did it
or1.why: A variant of the standard resurrection-to-deity argument.

or2.quote: Even critical scholars, Dale Allison, I mean others, uh, they think it's likely that Jesus foretold his death and resurrection ahead of time.
or2.why: Uses critical-scholarship concession as new support.

arguments.weakest_link: P4 ('God would not raise a false teacher') is a theological intuition, not evidence.
arguments.develop_next: Argue explicitly why divine omnibenevolence rules out raising a false teacher.

arguments.name: Scripture is entailed by the resurrection
arguments.conclusion: Scripture is entailed by the resurrection, though further down the line than the kingdom and ethics.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1 If Jesus is Lord and was raised, his view of Scripture ought to be obeyed.
P2 Jesus' two greatest commandments concern loving God and loving others, and Scripture follows from accepting his teaching.
P3 God did not raise Jesus merely to affirm a view of the Bible, but Scripture is still entailed somewhere down the line.

st1.quote: I think scriptures entailed somewhere down the line, just like I think ethics are entailed somewhere down the line.

st2.quote: If he is our Lord that's a New Testament view I think if Jesus is our Lord then we should take his view on things.

st3.quote: Jesus only numbers the two greatest theological doctrines in Luke 10.

st4.quote: I think scriptures down the line that Jesus's view of scripture ought to be obeyed.

st5.quote: I may upset some Christians by saying this, but I think scriptures entailed somewhere down the line

st6.quote: I don't think God raised him from the dead to say uh Jesus loves me this I know for the Bible tells me so.

st8.quote: If Jesus is our Lord then we should take his view on things.

or1.quote: I think scriptures entailed somewhere down the line
or1.why: A hierarchical entailment claim not standard in resurrection apologetics.

arguments.weakest_link: P1's move from 'Jesus is Lord' to 'obey his view of Scripture' needs an account of what Jesus' view was.
arguments.develop_next: Cite specific dominical texts on Scripture (e.g. Matt 5:17-18) to anchor the entailment.

arguments.name: Criteria for identifying a miracle
arguments.conclusion: A miracle is best identified as a one-time event, performed by God, with very good evidence, serving as a sign to authenticate a message.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1 A miracle is an act of God or an invisible agent, and by Christian standards such an agent is God or God's creation.
P2 Jesus taught that miracles are signs pointing to a truth, and he tied himself to that teaching.
P3 Richard Swinburne's definition is preferable: a miracle at its best is a one-time event with very good evidence, for the purpose of evidencing a message.
P4 Repeated events under known circumstances, such as alleged levitation, are not first-rate miracles.
P5 The resurrection fits this criterion uniquely because it is unrepeatable and was predicted ahead of time.

st1.quote: I like Richard Swinsburn's definition that a miracle it's it at its best it's a one-time event where the evidence is very good.

st2.quote: a miracle is an act of God or an invisible agent.

st3.quote: I think he said levitation might be a miracle.

st4.quote: if something is repeated under certain circumstances chances are that's not a miracle or if it is it's not a first rate miracle

st5.quote: some people say things like Richard Swinburn I think is a goes a little too far here

st6.quote: I think if something like that happened, yeah, it would be it would be the biggie, you know.

st7.quote: if you claim you're raised from the dead and you weren't, that's a big problem.

st8.quote: Even critical scholars, Dale Allison, I mean others, uh, they think it's likely that Jesus foretold his death and resurrection ahead of time.

arguments.prior_art: Richard Swinburne, The Concept of Miracle, 1970

or1.why: Adopts Swinburne's definition with a Habermas-specific application to the resurrection.

or2.quote: Even critical scholars, Dale Allison, I mean others, uh, they think it's likely that Jesus foretold his death and resurrection ahead of time.
or2.why: Adds critical-scholarship support for the prediction criterion.

or4.quote: I think he said levitation might be a miracle.
or4.why: Adds a repeatability criterion distinguishing first-rate from lesser miracles.

arguments.weakest_link: P1's identification of the invisible agent as God is assumed rather than argued.
arguments.develop_next: State independently checkable criteria for distinguishing divine acts from natural anomalies.
